title: Why Is the Sun Already Gone When You Watch It Set?
request: Biku's What's the Catch? script, used as it is: 'make a video for this script for whats the catch' (2026-10-18).
sources: David Basey, "Atmospheric Refraction", British Astronomical Association, 2 March 2019. Near the horizon the air lifts the Sun's image by about half a degree, roughly the Sun's apparent diameter; a Sun that seems to sit on the horizon is really below it; the lower edge is lifted more than the upper, so the disc looks oval. https://britastro.org/2019/atmospheric-refraction

Tong Yu-fai, "Effect of atmospheric refraction on the times of sunrise and sunset", Hong Kong Observatory, August 2017. Refraction makes sunset about 2 minutes later in Hong Kong than with no air (about 34 arcminutes of lift under average conditions); the published times already include it; the Sun truly disappears below the horizon before sunset happens. https://www.hko.gov.hk/en/education/astronomy-and-time/astronomy/00493-effect-of-atmospheric-refraction-on-the-times-of-sunrise-and-sunset.html
Checked by Claude against both pages on 2026-10-18.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Where is the Sun really when it touches the sea at sunset?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The answer is in the air around you, and it tricks your *eyes*.

shots.words: Where is the Sun really when it touches the sea at sunset?

overlay.text: Why Is the Sun Already Gone When You Watch It Set?

shots.words: The answer is in the air around you, and it tricks your *eyes*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You hold up your phone as the bottom of the Sun touches the sea.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Everyone filming thinks the Sun is right there, sitting on the water.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And they think its light flies to them in a *straight* line.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Both of those ideas are *wrong*.

shots.words: You hold up your phone as the bottom of the Sun touches the sea.
Everyone filming thinks the Sun is right there, sitting on the water.
And they think its light flies to them in a *straight* line.
Both of those ideas are *wrong*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The straw in the drink beside you shows why.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The straw looks snapped because light changes direction when it crosses from water into air.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Air bends light too, because air gets *thicker* the closer it is to the ground.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So sunlight curves a little as it passes down through each layer.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A high Sun's light comes almost straight down, so it barely bends.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But a low Sun's light skims sideways through the thickest air, so it bends the *most*.

shots.words: The straw in the drink beside you shows why.
The straw looks snapped because light changes direction when it crosses from water into air.
Air bends light too, because air gets *thicker* the closer it is to the ground.
So sunlight curves a little as it passes down through each layer.
A high Sun's light comes almost straight down, so it barely bends.
But a low Sun's light skims sideways through the thickest air, so it bends the *most*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Follow one beam from that low Sun as it curves down into your phone.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your eyes and your camera assume that light came in a *straight* line.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: But trace the curved beam back, and the real Sun is already *below* the horizon.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The air lifts the picture of the Sun by about its own *width*.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So the Sun on your screen has, in a way, already *set*.

shots.words: Follow one beam from that low Sun as it curves down into your phone.
Your eyes and your camera assume that light came in a *straight* line.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The British Astronomical Association puts that lift at about half a degree, roughly one whole Sun.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The Hong Kong Observatory says this makes sunset there about two minutes *later* than with no air.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And official sunset times already include those extra minutes.

shots.words: The British Astronomical Association puts that lift at about half a degree, roughly one whole Sun.
The Hong Kong Observatory says this makes sunset there about two minutes *later* than with no air.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You'll also notice a low Sun looks squashed, flat at the bottom.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the air lifting its bottom edge more than its top.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: So when the Sun touches the sea, the real Sun is already just *below* it.
